query: Earlier studies reported high hardness and compressive strength in AlCrCuFeNiTi, CuFeNiMnTi, and low-density AlCrFeTiX high-entropy alloys. However, some AlCrFeTiX alloys were brittle at 25 °C, and AlCrFeTiCo showed only 1.8% plastic strain at 600 °C. Because these findings concern different alloy systems, they do not explain the deformation behavior or the relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid-solution state, despite its favorable plasticity and machinability. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs this combination of deformation, hardness, and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting alloy, state the composition, state, temperature, and loading limits of the hypothesis, identify the prior evidence supporting its premise, and specify results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The relatively low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its simple solid‐solution state is governed by the absence of nanoscale obstacles—such as precipitates or short-range ordering—that would normally impede dislocation glide. In other words, without the dispersive or interfacial barriers present in multiphase or chemically ordered alloys, dislocations can move with fewer constraints, leading to high ductility and machinability at the expense of higher yield strength and hardness.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a single-phase, solid-solution state (with no significant nanoscale precipitates or ordering features) prepared by conventional casting or solution processing at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heat treatment (annealing followed by aging) to induce nanoscale precipitates or to enhance short-range chemical ordering without changing the overall equimolar composition.
generation.conditions: Test under quasi-static tensile and compressive loading at room temperature (approximately 25 °C) with strain rates typical for mechanical testing. Microstructural characterization (TEM, XRD, or atom probe) should confirm the presence or absence of nanoscale obstacles.
generation.structural_mediator: The generation (or absence) of nanoscale precipitates and/or enhanced short-range order that act as barriers to dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: In the as-cast simple solid solution, dislocation motion is relatively unimpeded due to low lattice distortion and lack of secondary phases. Controlled heat treatment that produces nanoscale precipitates or ordering will force dislocations to interact with these obstacles, thereby increasing yield strength and hardness but reducing ductility somewhat.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the starting alloy, samples with induced nanoscale precipitates/ordering should exhibit a higher yield strength and hardness. The ductility may decrease relative to the unmodified state, confirming that the mechanical properties can be tuned by tailoring the obstacle density within the alloy.
generation.baseline: Mechanical properties (hardness, yield strength, ductility) of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in its as-cast, simple solid-solution state at room temperature under quasi-static loading.
generation.boundary: Composition: equimolar Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Ti (each ~20 at.%); temperature: room temperature (~25 °C); loading: quasi-static tensile and compressive tests up to yielding; microstructure: single-phase solid solution vs. one with controlled nanoscale precipitates.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of strength/hardness increase will depend on the volume fraction, size, and distribution of the induced precipitates or ordering domains. Additionally, the impact on ductility may vary, and the optimal heat treatment parameters need to be determined empirically.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi samples: one set as-cast to maintain the simple solid-solution state, and a second set that undergoes a controlled annealing and aging treatment aimed at inducing nanoscale precipitates or a measurable short-range order. Characterize both sets using TEM, XRD, and/or atom probe tomography to confirm differences in microstructure. Then, perform quasi-static tensile and compressive tests at room temperature to compare hardness, yield strength, and ductility.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (TEM, XRD, APT) to verify the presence/absence of nanoscale obstacles
Uniaxial tensile and compressive tests for yield strength and ductility
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not show a statistically significant increase in hardness and yield strength relative to the as-cast simple solid solution, or if they do not display the predicted reduction in ductility (or show unexpected trends), then the hypothesis that the absence of nanoscale obstacles governs the low hardness and strength is falsified.

Dislocations and deformation microstructure in a B2-ordered Al28Co20Cr11Fe15Ni26 high-entropy alloy

Abstract: High-entropy alloys are multicomponent metallic materials currently attracting high research interest. They display a unique combination of chemical disorder and crystalline long-range order, and due to their attractive properties are promising candidates for technological application. Many high-entropy alloys possess surprisingly high strength, occasionally in combination with high ductility and low density. The mechanisms effecting these attractive mechanical properties are not understood. This study addresses the deformation mechanism of a Al28Co20Cr11Fe15Ni26 high-entropy alloy, which is a two-phase material, consisting of a B2-ordered matrix and disordered body-centred inclusions. We quantitatively analyse the microstructure and dislocations in deformed samples by transmission-electron-microscopic methods including weak-beam imaging and convergent-beam electron diffraction. Nanoindentation behavior of high entropy alloys with transformation-induced plasticity

Abstract: Nanoindentation of three metastable dual-phase high entropy alloys (HEAs) was performed to obtain their inherent elastoplastic deformation responses. Excellent combination of hardness and elastic modulus in as-cast condition confirmed that, their inherently higher strength compared to other HEAs reported in literature, can be attributed to alloy chemistry induced phase stability. Further, hardness of 8.28 GPa combined with modulus of 221.8 GPa was obtained in Fe-Mn-Co-Cr-Si-Cu HEA by annealing the as-cast material, which is the best hardness-modulus combination obtained to date in HEAs from nanoindentation. On the other hand, although Fe-Mn-Co-Cr-Si HEA showed lower hardness and modulus than Fe-Mn-Co-Cr-Si-Al and Fe-Mn-Co-Cr-Si-Cu HEAs, the former alloy exhibited the highest strain rate sensitivity, as determined from tests performed at five different strain rates.
